title: History and Standards
reading: You wrote a file-copy program on Linux and want to build it on another UNIX system. This chapter asks which parts of that move have a written promise behind them.
summary: You wrote a file-copy program on Linux and want to build it on another UNIX system.
prompt: A program works on Linux. What would make you confident it also works on another UNIX system?
explanation: A function name tells the compiler which operation you want, but the spelling alone does not say how every system implements it. Documentation specifies acceptable inputs, results and failures. That promise is an interface contract; an API is a collection of such programming interfaces.

POSIX is a family of standards describing many UNIX interfaces. Depending on a POSIX interface such as read can help source portability: the ability to rebuild source on another conforming system. Linux-only interfaces such as epoll require a different plan on other systems.

A compiled executable has additional machine and library requirements. Their binary calling and data-layout rules form an ABI. Source portability therefore does not promise that you can copy a Linux executable to another operating system and run it. Read the chapter’s history as an explanation of why these different promises exist.
follow_up: What evidence would you want before calling a program portable?

title: Fundamental Concepts
reading: You ask a shell to start a program. A shell is itself a running program that accepts commands. Follow what the newly started program needs before asking what it is allowed to access.
summary: You ask a shell to start a program.
prompt: A hypothetical child changes its private integer. Does that tell you whether it can read a file?
explanation: A program stored in an executable file contains instructions and starting data. When those instructions run, Linux maintains a running instance called a process. Starting the same executable twice can produce two processes with different working information. The kernel is the core part of the operating system that manages resources and handles requests from running programs.

A process uses memory to keep that working information. An ordinary C integer variable keeps a whole-number value in part of that memory. Private memory lets a process change its working information independently of another process; explicit shared memory is a different case.

Here is a preview of the separate Lab 001 example, not an experiment performed by reading this guide. One process has an ordinary private integer containing 42. A successful ordinary fork() creates a child process. The original process is called the parent. Both parent and child continue after the call with that starting value. If the child assigns 7 to its private integer, the parent’s integer remains 42. This example concerns an ordinary private variable, not shared memory.

Memory and permission are separate questions. The child can have independent private variables while retaining access to files the parent already opened. Credentials are the kernel’s user/group identity and related permission information for a process. An open file descriptor is a small number through which the process uses an already-open resource. Neither is removed merely by giving the child private memory. A file read depends on the access the child retains and the checks relevant to that operation.
follow_up: When a process executes a different program, which resources would you expect it to retain?

concepts.title: Optional depth: addresses and copy-on-write
concepts.scenario: The parent and child start with the same private integer value, yet later writes can differ.
concepts.explanation: A process refers to memory using addresses, values that locate storage from its own point of view. The range and arrangement of memory it can address is its virtual address space, not a list of files it may open. Linux can initially let separate private mappings use the same underlying physical pages and arrange separation when a private write requires it. That technique is called copy-on-write. The ordinary-variable behavior does not require eagerly copying every physical page when fork creates the child.
concepts.assumptions: This explanation concerns ordinary private memory after successful fork. It is optional implementation depth beyond the preview; reading it supplies neither a runtime observation nor a reviewed source visit.
concepts.counterexample: An explicitly shared mapping can let one process’s writes become visible to another. Separate private memory also does not remove inherited file access.

title: System Programming Concepts
reading: A program tries to open an input file that may not exist. Before it can recover, it needs a reliable way to tell failure from a usable result.
summary: A program tries to open an input file that may not exist.
prompt: A call reports failure. Is printing a generic error enough to understand what happened?
explanation: A call’s return value is its immediate report to the expression that called it. For open, a nonnegative integer is a usable file descriptor, and -1 indicates failure. Other interfaces use different conventions, so begin with that interface’s documented result.

After a documented failure, errno can supply an error number explaining its cause. A previous error number may remain after a later successful call. Reading errno without first checking the result can therefore describe an unrelated old failure.

A C type says what kind of value is expected, such as an integer. Headers supply declarations, including types and function signatures. A feature-test macro is a source setting that changes which declarations a header exposes; it belongs before the includes. This chapter helps you read manual-page prototypes, match argument types, and keep useful context such as the failed pathname when reporting errors.
follow_up: What information would make a failed open useful to diagnose later?

title: File I/O: The Universal I/O Model
reference: Chapter 4 · File I/O: The Universal I/O Model · pp. 69–88
reading: A copy program asks for a block of input and receives fewer bytes than it requested. It must decide what to copy and whether to ask again.
summary: A copy program asks for a block of input and receives fewer bytes than it requested.
prompt: Your copy program asks to read 4096 bytes and receives only 700. Has it reached the end?
explanation: Opening a resource returns a file descriptor: a small integer the process supplies to later I/O calls. The descriptor is a handle to an open resource, not the resource’s contents. read places bytes into a buffer and returns how many it placed there.

If a request for 4096 bytes returns 700, only those 700 bytes are new input. That is a partial transfer. It does not by itself mean the input ended. For a regular file, read returning zero indicates end of file, often abbreviated EOF; errors use the documented failure result instead.

write also returns an actual count. If it accepts only part of a buffer, advance past that part and keep the rest for another attempt. The chapter builds a universal way to reason about many resources through these calls, while each resource still has its own blocking, end-of-input and error rules.
follow_up: If write accepts only part of your buffer, where should the next write begin?

concepts.title: Advance through a real buffer
concepts.scenario: read supplies 700 bytes into a 4096-byte buffer.
concepts.explanation: After a positive read count, maintain an offset into the initialized portion of the buffer. Add each positive write count to the offset; never pass the entire buffer capacity as though every byte were input.
concepts.assumptions: A byte buffer has a known capacity and each successful count advances within its bounds.
concepts.counterexample: Writing sizeof(buffer) would include bytes that were not supplied by this read.
concepts.code_context: Inside a copy loop with owned out, a valid buffer and a positive read count n. Setup, full error reporting and descriptor cleanup are not included; this is not a runnable copy program.
concepts.code_syntax: size_t holds nonnegative sizes; ssize_t can also hold the failure value -1. buffer + offset points past bytes already sent. += advances offset only by a positive returned count. The cast uses n only after it is known positive.

concepts.title: Interruption and cleanup
concepts.scenario: A copy loop is interrupted while waiting for input.
concepts.explanation: An interrupted call can report -1 with EINTR, meaning a signal interrupted the request. Retry according to that operation’s contract; positive progress remains progress. The regular-file example does not define a nonblocking socket’s EAGAIN policy.
concepts.assumptions: The copy loop owns both descriptors; an interrupted operation may have transferred bytes if its return count says so.
concepts.counterexample: Blind retries of every error can loop forever; this regular-file copy example does not define nonblocking EAGAIN policy.

title: File I/O: Further Details
reference: Chapter 5 · File I/O: Further Details · pp. 89–112
reading: A program opens a file and duplicates the resulting descriptor. It now has two numbers it can use to read, but that does not necessarily mean two independent reading positions.
summary: A program opens a file and duplicates the resulting descriptor.
prompt: Two descriptors refer to one open file description. Which changes can one user see through the other?
explanation: A process has entries that map descriptor numbers to open resources. A successful dup creates another descriptor entry pointing to the same underlying open-file record. That record is called an open file description; it contains the current file offset and file status flags.

If descriptor A reads ten bytes, descriptor B’s next ordinary read uses the advanced offset when both refer to that same description. Closing A removes A’s entry; B can remain usable. Opening the file independently is a contrasting case that normally creates a new description with its own offset.

Some flags belong to the individual descriptor entry instead. Close-on-exec is such a flag: it tells Linux to close that entry when the process successfully replaces its program. The chapter’s extra I/O interfaces make sense once you ask which record each operation changes.
follow_up: Would two independent open calls share the same offset?

concepts.explanation: dup shares an open file description; another open of the same pathname normally does not. Equal offsets observed once do not prove sharing. The shared-offset investigation is a separate program for observing that distinction.
concepts.assumptions: The duplicate comes from dup of an existing descriptor, rather than a second open.
concepts.counterexample: Equal numeric offsets observed once do not demonstrate that two descriptions are shared.

concepts.title: Positioned I/O
concepts.scenario: One component needs bytes at an explicit offset while another reads sequentially.
concepts.explanation: pread takes an explicit position and does not change the description’s current offset. That removes one source of offset interference on a seekable file, but concurrent writers can still change the bytes or file size.
concepts.assumptions: Use a seekable regular file and explicit offsets; pread does not alter its open-file description’s current offset.
concepts.counterexample: Concurrent writers can still change the file contents or size; pread is not a snapshot or lock.

title: Processes
reading: You start the same command twice with different filenames. Each running copy needs to remember which input it was given.
summary: You start the same command twice with different filenames.
prompt: Why can two running copies of the same executable have different environments and arguments?
explanation: A launcher supplies argument strings when starting a program. In a C main that accepts them, argc counts those strings and argv lets the program locate them. Two processes running the same executable can receive different arguments.

The launcher also supplies named strings called environment variables. A program may use them for settings such as language or search paths. They are inputs, not proof of who launched the process or what access it should have.

Within the process, memory areas support different lifetimes: automatic local variables are associated with active function calls, while dynamically allocated blocks remain until released. A process ID, or PID, identifies a running process under the system’s rules. It is not a permanent identity for an executable or a person. This chapter connects startup inputs and memory organization to that running instance.

title: Memory Allocation
reading: A program needs a buffer whose size is known only while it runs. Later it releases that buffer, but an old pointer still appears to locate the same bytes.
summary: A program needs a buffer whose size is known only while it runs.
prompt: A freed allocation still seems readable. Does that make using it valid?
explanation: malloc requests a block of storage and returns a pointer, or a failure result. Your program must decide which part of its code is responsible for eventually releasing that allocation. That responsibility is often called ownership.

free ends the allocation’s lifetime: the interval in which using that allocated object is valid. The allocator may keep the underlying memory available for later allocations. An old pointer appearing to work after free does not extend the object’s lifetime; using it is invalid C behavior.

realloc can resize a nonzero allocation by returning a new pointer. Keep the original pointer until you know that request succeeded. A failed request leaves the original allocation available, whereas overwriting your only pointer with the failure result can lose your way to release it. This chapter separates program-level storage management from Linux’s management of memory pages.

concepts.title: Do not lose the original allocation
concepts.scenario: realloc fails while expanding a nonzero-sized buffer.
concepts.explanation: For a validated nonzero size, store realloc’s result in a temporary pointer. Update the owning pointer only after a non-null result. Check multiplication/addition used to compute sizes before allocating.
concepts.assumptions: The request has nonzero size and the caller still owns the old allocation when realloc fails.
concepts.counterexample: Assigning realloc directly to the sole owner pointer can leak the old allocation on failure.
concepts.code_context: buffer is the still-owned allocation and new_size is validated and nonzero. Surrounding allocation, use and final free are not shown.
concepts.code_syntax: void * can hold a pointer to an allocated object. = initializes replacement with the result; != compares it to the null pointer NULL. Updating buffer only on success preserves the original owner on failure. A null pointer identifies no allocated object.

concepts.title: Mapped is not owned
concepts.scenario: A freed pointer still appears readable in a debugger.
concepts.explanation: An allocator can reuse a freed block without unmapping its pages. A page being mapped and readable is a kernel-level access fact; it does not establish the lifetime or bounds of a C allocation.
concepts.assumptions: A successful mapping has a separately tracked length and lifetime; C allocation ownership is a caller discipline.
concepts.counterexample: A successful read of stale storage is not evidence that accessing it is valid or isolated from other objects.

title: Users and Groups
reading: A directory listing displays an owner’s name. The account is renamed, and you want to know whether every file must change ownership.
summary: A directory listing displays an owner’s name.
prompt: A file stores a numeric owner ID. What happens if the account name changes?
explanation: Linux records user identity with numeric user IDs, called UIDs, and group identity with group IDs, called GIDs. Files can store these numbers as ownership information. Names are a way for people to look up or display those IDs.

An account lookup translates between a name and an account record. It may consult local files or configured network services. A missing display name does not erase a file’s numeric owner, and a failed lookup must not be treated as a successful identity check.

Looking up a name also does not prove that a requester controls that account. Proving identity is authentication; deciding whether an identified requester may perform an operation is authorization. This chapter supplies the account-data background for the access checks studied next.

title: Process Credentials
reading: A program wants to open a file. Printing an account name is not enough to explain which identity the system uses for that request.
summary: A program wants to open a file.
prompt: A program has a real user ID and an effective user ID. Which one explains its current access?
explanation: The kernel keeps identity information for a process. These credentials include several IDs with different jobs. The real user ID records one aspect of the process’s identity history; the effective user ID is used by many permission-related decisions.

For example, a set-user-ID executable is configured so execution may select the file owner’s user ID as effective, subject to the system’s execution rules. That effective ID can differ from the caller’s real ID. Additional group memberships, called supplementary groups, can affect access too. This is why one printed ID cannot explain every permission check.

Changing an effective ID is not necessarily irreversible. A saved ID can permit certain later identity changes. Linux also has filesystem IDs and more detailed privilege rules. The chapter teaches you to name the actual operation and inspect the credentials relevant to it before claiming that privilege has been removed.

title: Time
reading: A download takes ten seconds on your watch but uses little processor time. Both observations can be correct.
summary: A download takes ten seconds on your watch but uses little processor time.
prompt: A clock is adjusted while you measure a task. Could the measured duration become misleading?
explanation: Calendar time answers a human question such as the date a log entry was made. That clock can be adjusted. Subtracting two calendar readings can therefore be a poor way to measure how long an operation took.

An elapsed interval needs a clock suited to durations. A monotonic clock does not jump backward when calendar time is reset, though its exact sleep/suspend and adjustment behavior depends on the chosen clock. Take both measurements from the same clock.

CPU time measures execution consumed rather than all time spent waiting. A process waiting for network input may accumulate much less CPU time than elapsed time. This chapter also teaches timestamp representations: seconds and smaller units must be combined and subtracted consistently.

title: File I/O Buffering
reading: A program prints a message, but redirected output is not immediately visible in its destination file. Later you also want to know whether it would survive a crash.
summary: A program prints a message, but redirected output is not immediately visible in its destination file.
prompt: A printf succeeds and then power is lost. Were the bytes necessarily saved?
explanation: stdio functions such as printf can first collect characters in a user-space buffer: memory managed by the library inside the process. This saves repeated small output requests. A successful printf need not mean the kernel has received those bytes yet.

fflush asks the library to send its pending output onward. The kernel and storage device can have their own pending work. Acceptance into one layer is different from persistence, meaning survival under the failures covered by a storage contract.

fsync addresses file synchronization rather than the stdio buffer alone; it has its own failure handling and filesystem implications. This chapter separates those stages so you can decide which result you need. Forking with pending stdio output adds another issue: both processes can inherit copies of that buffer and later emit the same characters.

title: File Systems

explanation: A filesystem organizes stored objects and directories. A directory entry associates a name with an object; more than one entry can refer to the same file. Such additional entries are hard links.

Opening a name obtains a reference that a process can use through a descriptor. Removing one name with unlink does not remove every other link or already-open reference. The file’s storage can remain needed while those references survive.

title: File Attributes
reading: A program checks a pathname, then opens it. Someone able to change the directory may replace that name between the two requests.

prompt: A program checks permissions, then opens the file. Can the file change between those steps?
explanation: A stat-style request obtains metadata for the object reached during that request. That information can help answer whether the object has the expected type or size. It does not freeze the pathname for the next operation.

A later open performs another name lookup and may reach a different object. This gap between checking and using is a race: the outcome depends on another action that can occur between yours. Where appropriate, open with a suitable strategy and inspect that opened reference using fstat.

Basic permission bits describe read, write and execute for the file’s owner, a group class and an other class. These are different sets of possible rights, not three successive steps that every requester automatically receives. Additional rules can affect the complete access decision.

Permission bits also name particular operations. On a directory, read concerns listing names, search concerns traversing a component when a name is known, and write participates in changing directory entries. This chapter connects attributes to the operation being attempted rather than treating a permission display as a universal yes/no label.

title: Access Control Lists
reading: A colleague is named in a file permission list, but a write request is still denied. The displayed grant has another limit to account for.
summary: A colleague is named in a file permission list, but a write request is still denied.
prompt: An ACL entry names a user, yet access is narrower than that entry appears to allow. Why?
explanation: An access control list, or ACL, adds named user and group entries to the basic owner/group/other permission model. It lets a file describe more cases than one owning group alone.

Some entries are limited by another entry called the mask. If a named user entry contains read and write but the mask permits only read, that user’s effective permissions through that entry are read only. Effective here means the permissions that remain after the mask is applied.

The owner and other entries are not limited by this mask. Group matching has its own rules, so an ACL is not a list of grants to add indiscriminately. A directory’s default ACL concerns initializing new children; its access ACL concerns using the directory itself. This chapter teaches you to distinguish these decisions before predicting a result.

nodes.label: Matching group grants requested rights, within mask if present

nodes.label: No matched class: other permissions, unmasked

concepts.explanation: A default ACL on a directory participates in initializing a new child’s permissions together with creation-mode rules. It is different from that directory’s own access ACL and does not retroactively rewrite every existing child.
concepts.assumptions: A default directory ACL affects creation; existing children require separate inspection.
concepts.counterexample: A child's later ACL is not a live reference automatically tracking every future change to its parent's default ACL.

title: Directories and Links
reading: A file has another hard-link name and a symbolic-link name. You rename the original and want to know which references still work.

title: Signals: Fundamental Concepts
reading: You press Ctrl+C while a program runs in a terminal. The program often ends, but the key press and the program’s response are different parts of the story.
summary: You press Ctrl+C while a program runs in a terminal.
prompt: In the one-thread example, SIGINT is not ignored but is blocked when you press Ctrl+C. Has the process discarded it?
explanation: Under the usual terminal configuration, Ctrl+C causes the terminal to send SIGINT, an interrupt signal, to its foreground process group. This is the group of processes currently selected to interact with that terminal; it can contain more than one process, such as the members of a pipeline. A signal is a notification managed by the kernel. Different terminal settings can change what Ctrl+C does.

SIGINT’s default action is termination: ending the process. A program can instead arrange a permitted response, such as running a handler function or ignoring SIGINT. This choice of action is called the signal’s disposition. The terminal sends the signal; it does not decide which response each program has configured.

Sending SIGINT in this example generates a signal for each targeted process. Generation means the request has been created. Delivery is the handling step at which Linux applies the signal’s action; it need not happen at the key press. Keeping these steps separate lets us ask whether a generated signal is waiting to be handled.

Consider one targeted process with one thread, meaning one execution path. The thread can temporarily block SIGINT using its signal mask, the set of signal numbers it blocks. If SIGINT is not ignored, it can remain pending: generated but not yet delivered. Unblocking makes it eligible for delivery again. Blocking postpones delivery; ignoring chooses to discard the signal instead. Masks belong to individual threads, so a process with several threads needs the additional targeting rules in the optional depth.

Not every signal permits these choices. SIGKILL and SIGSTOP cannot be caught, blocked or ignored. Repeated standard signals such as SIGINT can combine into one pending indication, so repeated key presses do not provide an unlimited event count. The chapter uses this distinction between a request, its delivery and its configured action to explain signal behavior.

title: Signals: Signal Handlers
reading: A program is formatting output when a signal handler runs. Calling the same output machinery from the handler can interrupt unfinished internal work.

prompt: Why is calling a convenient library function from a signal handler sometimes dangerous?
explanation: Library operations may temporarily update shared internal records in several steps. If a handler calls into that machinery before the interrupted operation finishes, it may encounter inconsistent state or wait for a lock the interrupted code cannot release yet.

An async-signal-safe interface has a documented contract for use from this interruption context. That is stronger than being safe for ordinary concurrent threads. printf and allocation routines must not be assumed safe in a handler.

title: Process Creation
reading: A C program has a private integer containing 42. It asks Linux to create a child and needs to decide what each process should do next.

prompt: After fork, are the parent and child taking turns inside one copy of a variable?
explanation: On successful fork(), the original parent and the new child both continue after the call. The child does not restart main. Each receives a different returned value: zero in the child and the child’s positive process ID in the parent. A failure reports -1 in the parent and creates no child.

Branches let the two successful processes do different work. If the child assigns 7 to its ordinary private integer, that does not update the parent’s integer. The initial value is the same; subsequent private changes are independent.

The process’s view of addressable memory is its virtual address space. Linux commonly implements private memory after fork using copy-on-write: physical storage may initially be shared, with copying deferred until private writes need separation. That implementation does not change the private-variable contract. summary: A parent has children doing work.
prompt: A wait call returns a status integer. Is that integer simply the child's exit code?
explanation: waitpid reports which requested child supplied a state change through its return value. Separately, it can write encoded information into an integer the parent provides. In C, &status means the address of that integer, allowing the function to fill it.

That encoded wait status must first be classified. WIFEXITED asks whether the child exited normally; only then should WEXITSTATUS extract a normal exit code. Signal termination has a different test and extraction operation.

With WNOHANG, the wait need not block: zero means no requested report is available now. A positive result identifies a reported child; -1 means an error. The chapter teaches both the reporting variants and who owns the responsibility to wait, without assuming every report means termination.
follow_up: How would your handling differ for a child killed by a signal?

title: Program Execution
reading: A launcher has created a child and wants that child to run a different executable. It must prepare the new program’s inputs before replacing its own code.
summary: A launcher has created a child and wants that child to run a different executable.
prompt: If exec succeeds, where does the next line of the old program run?
explanation: An exec interface asks to replace the calling process’s program image: its executable instructions and associated user-space program state. A successful exec does not create a new PID and does not return to the next instruction of the old program.

The new program receives chosen argument and environment strings. For execve, these are supplied through arrays of pointers: sequences whose elements locate strings, with a null pointer marking the end. An empty string is still a string, not that end marker.

Failure leaves the old image available to handle the returned error. Success retains some process properties, including open descriptors unless close-on-exec applies. This chapter therefore connects program replacement to deliberate launch preparation; replacing code does not erase every existing resource or identity.

title: Process Creation and Program Execution in More Detail
reference: Chapter 28 · Process Creation and Program Execution in More Detail · pp. 591–616
reading: A parent starts a child that tries exec. The parent needs to distinguish a reported launch error from successful startup and later application readiness.
summary: A parent starts a child that tries exec.
prompt: How can a launcher distinguish a successful exec from a child that exits immediately?
explanation: A pipe is a byte channel with a reading end and a writing end. A child can use its writing end to report a returning exec error to the parent. Marking that end close-on-exec makes successful exec close it automatically.

The parent can see end of input, or EOF, only after all writing references are gone and queued bytes have been consumed. Each process must close its unused ends. An accidental retained writer can prevent the parent from seeing the expected end.

EOF alone is not absolute proof that exec succeeded: the child could die before reporting. Combine the reporting protocol with child status and, if needed, a separate message that the new application is ready. This chapter brings the launch mechanisms together while distinguishing prepared inputs from actual confinement.

title: Threads: Introduction
reading: A program starts a worker while its original execution path continues. The worker is given a pointer to an integer that both paths can reach.
summary: A program starts a worker while its original execution path continues.
prompt: Two threads update the same object. Does having separate stacks make the object private?
explanation: Threads in one process share its addressable memory and many resources. Creating a thread does not make a private copy of every variable as ordinary fork does. If two threads hold pointers to the same integer, they can reach that same object.

Each thread has a stack for its active function calls, but another thread can still reach stack storage through a valid pointer. The object must remain alive until the worker has stopped using it. A separate stack is not an access barrier.

Joining a thread waits for its termination and allows collection of its result under the interface contract. In the optional illustration, the original thread joins before reading the updated integer or leaving its scope. This chapter introduces execution and lifetime; Chapter 30 adds coordination for concurrently accessed shared state.

title: Threads: Thread Synchronization
reading: A consumer wants an item from a shared queue. It must avoid taking an item that is not there or missing a producer’s change while it starts waiting.
summary: A consumer wants an item from a shared queue.
prompt: In a faulty approach, a consumer checks the queue while holding the mutex, finds it empty, unlocks the mutex, and separately starts waiting for a notification. Where could a producer add an item and send a notification, leaving the consumer waiting despite available work?
explanation: A mutex is a lock that cooperating threads use to take turns inspecting and changing shared state. While holding the queue’s mutex, the consumer checks whether an item is available. That true/false condition is called a predicate.

If the queue is empty, pthread_cond_wait() coordinates releasing the mutex and waiting for a notification. Before returning it reacquires the mutex. Compare a faulty approach: the consumer unlocks first and only afterward starts waiting. In that gap, a producer can acquire the mutex, add an item and notify before the consumer is waiting. A condition variable does not keep that notification for a future waiter. The coordinated release-and-wait avoids this gap when participants inspect and change the same predicate under the same mutex.

The consumer checks the predicate again in a while loop after every return. This solves a separate problem: a wakeup does not reserve an item, another consumer may have taken it, and wakeups can occur without the predicate becoming true. The loop alone cannot repair an incorrectly separated unlock-and-wait operation. The lock protects the queue state, coordinated waiting avoids the start-waiting gap, and the loop checks whether work is actually available after waking.

orientation.heading: Wait for a condition, then check it again
orientation.prerequisite: Recall shared objects between threads. A queue is stored program data containing items to process; concurrent changes need a coordinated rule.

reflection_answer: The producer can act after the consumer unlocks but before the consumer starts waiting: it locks the mutex, adds an item, sends a notification and unlocks. If no one is waiting yet, that notification is not saved for the later waiter. The consumer can then sleep with an item already in the queue. Instead, call pthread_cond_wait() while holding the mutex: it coordinates releasing that mutex with starting the wait. When the producer follows the same mutex/predicate protocol, its notification after acquiring the released mutex behaves as if the consumer were already waiting. After the wait returns with the mutex held, the while loop rechecks the queue for a different reason: waking does not guarantee an item is still available. The loop does not reserve an item or fix the faulty separated operation.
security_connection: A mutex coordinates threads that follow its protocol; it does not deny file or network access to a thread running the same program. Protecting a queue’s consistency and limiting a worker’s authority are different design tasks.

title: Threads: Thread Safety and Per-Thread Storage
reference: Chapter 31 · Threads: Thread Safety and Per-Thread Storage · pp. 655–670
reading: A function returns a pointer to formatted text. Another thread calls that function before the first thread finishes using the text.
summary: A function returns a pointer to formatted text.
prompt: A function returns a pointer to static storage. What if another thread calls it before you use the result?
explanation: Some interfaces return a pointer to reusable internal storage. Two callers can hold different local pointer variables but still refer to the same underlying bytes. A later call may replace those bytes.

A thread-safe interface promises suitable concurrent use under its documented conditions. Caller-supplied-buffer alternatives can give each caller its own result storage, but their exact result and sizing rules still need reading.

Thread-specific storage provides a separate value for a key in each thread. That can keep each thread’s pointer slot separate; it does not automatically duplicate the object those pointers reach. This chapter helps you inspect both internal library state and the ownership of returned data.

concepts.counterexample: Per-thread storage does not automatically deep-copy an object graph or make an unsafe library algorithm safe.

title: Threads: Thread Cancellation
reading: A worker has taken a lock and acquired resources when another thread asks it to stop. Leaving those resources in an unfinished state can block later work.
summary: A worker has taken a lock and acquired resources when another thread asks it to stop.
prompt: A thread is canceled while holding a mutex. Who releases the mutex?
explanation: Thread cancellation is a request that can end a thread under the cancellation rules. With deferred cancellation, the request takes effect at specified opportunities called cancellation points, rather than at every possible instruction.

A worker must account for resources held when it can be canceled. Cleanup handlers are registered actions used during cancellation to release resources or restore an agreed state. They do not invent the correct recovery rule for partially changed application data.

A cooperative stop protocol is another option: normal code observes a synchronized stop request, wakes if necessary and cleans up deliberately. Asynchronous cancellation is much harder to make safe because it can interrupt unfinished operations at less controlled points. This chapter develops these choices rather than treating termination as automatic cleanup.

title: Threads: Further Details
reading: A thread calls fork while another thread holds a library lock. The child can inherit memory describing that lock without inheriting the thread that would release it.
summary: A thread calls fork while another thread holds a library lock.
prompt: After a multithreaded process forks, who can unlock a mutex held by a thread that was not copied?
explanation: In the child of a multithreaded process, only the thread that called fork continues. Other threads from the parent do not resume there. The child’s copied memory can nevertheless contain records left by those threads, including a locked mutex.

If child code then calls a library function needing that lock, it may have no surviving thread able to release it. This is a concrete reason POSIX restricts the child before exec to async-signal-safe operations: operations with the required interruption-safety contract discussed in Chapter 21.

Fork preparation/parent/child hooks can coordinate specific known state, but they cannot automatically repair arbitrary library locks. This chapter examines those interactions and the distinction between process-wide operations and per-thread state. Prefer a documented, narrow launch path rather than assuming fork makes a multithreaded program start fresh.

title: Process Groups, Sessions, and Job Control
reference: Chapter 34 · Process Groups, Sessions, and Job Control · pp. 699–732
reading: A shell starts two commands joined by a pipe. Pressing Ctrl-C can affect both commands, even though the shell remains available for the next command.
summary: A shell starts two commands joined by a pipe.
prompt: Why can pressing Ctrl-C affect every program in a pipeline instead of only the shell?
explanation: A process group collects related processes, such as the members of a shell pipeline. It has an identifying number distinct from each process’s role as parent or child.

A terminal records which process group is its foreground group. Under the terminal’s configured rules, characters such as Ctrl-C generate a signal for that foreground group. The terminal is not choosing targets by walking the parent-child tree.

A session groups a broader set of process groups and can have a controlling terminal. The shell uses these relationships to move jobs between foreground and background and to observe stopping, continuation and termination. This chapter supplies that structure; the later terminal chapters explain the input-processing details.

title: Process Priorities and Scheduling
reference: Chapter 35 · Process Priorities and Scheduling · pp. 733–752
reading: A high-priority worker waits for disk input while another worker can execute. Higher priority does not make missing input arrive sooner.
summary: A high-priority worker waits for disk input while another worker can execute.
prompt: A worker has a higher scheduling priority. Does that guarantee it finishes before a lower-priority worker?
explanation: The scheduler chooses which eligible runnable tasks receive CPU time. A task blocked waiting for I/O or a lock is not runnable merely because its priority is high.

A scheduling policy defines how that choice is made. Normal nice values influence ordinary scheduling; real-time priorities belong to different policies with different rules and permission requirements. Neither name alone is a promise that one application finishes first.

Suppose a high-priority task needs a lock held by a lower-priority task. It depends on that owner making progress; this situation can produce priority inversion. The chapter connects policy and priority to actual dependencies, CPU placement and latency rather than treating a single number as a completion guarantee.

title: Daemons
reading: A service should keep running without an interactive terminal. It still needs somewhere to report errors and a way to handle shutdown.

prompt: A long-running service has no terminal. What now handles its shutdown and diagnostics?

title: Writing Secure Privileged Programs
reference: Chapter 38 · Writing Secure Privileged Programs · pp. 783–796
reading: A helper can modify a protected file for another program. Its caller supplies a pathname, so the helper must decide what request it is actually willing to perform.

prompt: A privileged helper checks a pathname and later opens it. Which input can change in between?
explanation: A privileged helper acts with access its caller may not possess. Before using that access, it needs a narrow definition of the permitted job: which object, which operation and which inputs are acceptable.

A pathname can change between a check and a later lookup. Inspecting an appropriately opened descriptor keeps subsequent inspection tied to that opened object, but the acquisition strategy must also avoid selecting an unintended object. Moving a check later cannot repair every unsafe open.

A threat model states which inputs or peers may be hostile and what must be protected from them. Keeping parsing outside a small privileged component and reducing its unnecessary access can make that model easier to examine. This chapter builds defensive responsibilities; it does not ask you to install a privileged helper or claim one check makes a sandbox.

title: Capabilities
reading: A service is not running as numeric user ID zero, yet a particular normally privileged operation succeeds. Its UID is not the whole explanation.
summary: A service is not running as numeric user ID zero, yet a particular normally privileged operation succeeds.
prompt: A process is not UID 0 but can perform a normally privileged operation. How could that happen?
explanation: Linux capabilities divide some traditionally privileged operations into named categories. A capability is relevant because a particular kernel check consults it; its presence is not universal permission to do everything.

A process has several capability sets with different transition roles. The effective set participates in checks, while other sets can affect what becomes effective later. Executing a program can change capability state according to process state, file metadata and restrictions.

The governing user namespace also matters: it scopes identity and many capability checks. A permission relevant in one namespace does not imply that the same action is authorized against resources governed elsewhere. title: Fundamentals of Shared Libraries
reference: Chapter 41 · Fundamentals of Shared Libraries · pp. 833–858
reading: An executable calls a function whose implementation is stored in a separate library file. Building the program and starting it involve different steps.
summary: An executable calls a function whose implementation is stored in a separate library file.
prompt: Why can a program start even though some of its function implementations are in another file?
explanation: Linking connects compiled code with the definitions or dependencies it needs. With a shared library, some implementation remains in a separate object that the runtime linker/loader finds when the program starts.

The executable and library must agree on binary calling and data-layout rules, their ABI. A matching filename does not make an incompatible function definition safe to call. A successful build also does not ensure every required runtime library will be found on another machine.

Library search paths are part of startup behavior. The optional two-file illustration shows building a small library and a caller, but is not an experiment you have run by reading it. This chapter connects compile-time declarations, link-time dependencies and runtime loading without treating them as one event.

title: Advanced Features of Shared Libraries
reference: Chapter 42 · Advanced Features of Shared Libraries · pp. 859–876
reading: A host program loads a plugin, finds an entry point and later unloads it. A saved callback still points toward the plugin’s code.

prompt: A plugin is unloaded while a callback still points into it. Is the callback still usable?
explanation: dlopen loads an object under the runtime loader’s rules. dlsym looks up a named symbol, such as a plugin entry point. The lookup result must be used with the documented compatible type, not guessed from the name.
Lookup has a particular error protocol: clear an earlier dlerror state, perform the lookup, then inspect dlerror. A null-valued symbol alone is not sufficient to decide that lookup failed.

Unloading requires a lifetime agreement. Stop new plugin calls, wait for current users and release plugin-owned data/callback references before unloading under the loader contract. Finding a symbol once does not make its code or data valid forever. This chapter develops those advanced linking responsibilities; a plugin runs code with the host’s context, not in a separate sandbox.

title: Interprocess Communication Overview
reading: Two processes need to exchange work. They might send bytes, send distinct messages or access storage mapped into both processes.
summary: Two processes need to exchange work.
prompt: Two processes need to exchange work. Should they share memory or send messages?
explanation: Interprocess communication, or IPC, names mechanisms for communication between processes. Begin with the application’s needs: what is sent, how a receiver knows a request is complete, and what happens when a peer stops.

A byte stream needs framing, a rule for finding message boundaries. A message queue supplies distinct records but has size and capacity rules. Shared memory gives processes access to common storage; it still needs coordination to prevent partially changed records being read.

Finite capacity also needs a policy. Slowing or rejecting new production when a receiver cannot keep up is backpressure. This chapter compares mechanisms by these obligations, not by assuming that one fast transport automatically solves the whole protocol.

concepts.explanation: VMIN/VTIME define noncanonical byte-count/timing behavior together with other flags. Clearing canonical mode alone does not remove every translation, echo rule or signal-generation behavior.
concepts.assumptions: Noncanonical settings still include VMIN/VTIME and other transformations; raw mode requires deliberate additional changes.
concepts.counterexample: Clearing one mode bit does not automatically supply a complete raw-terminal configuration.

orientation.heading: The terminal can process input before your program reads
orientation.prerequisite: Recall blocking reads and signals. A terminal has configurable input/output behavior separate from a program’s own buffer.

reflection_answer: Terminal line processing can retain input until the configured conditions are met. Echo can display characters independently of the application’s read.

title: Alternative I/O Models
reading: An event loop is told that a descriptor may be read. Another consumer or a state change can intervene before the loop attempts its read.
summary: An event loop is told that a descriptor may be read.
prompt: An event loop is told a descriptor is readable. Can its next read still require careful error handling?
explanation: Readiness interfaces let a program wait for descriptors with relevant conditions instead of trying every descriptor repeatedly. A readiness notification does not reserve the data for this particular reader.

A nonblocking read can return bytes, end of input, an error or EAGAIN: no progress available now under the nonblocking contract. Preserve partial data and handle those outcomes separately, even after notification.

Level-triggered reporting can repeat while the condition remains. With edge-triggered epoll, deliberately drain nonblocking input until EAGAIN, EOF or failure under the interface’s rules; leaving input unread may not produce another edge to wake the loop. This chapter compares alternative progress models, not a replacement for transfer-result checking.

concepts.title: Drain after an edge
concepts.scenario: An edge-triggered epoll event announces input.
concepts.explanation: For edge-triggered epoll, use nonblocking descriptors and drain available work while preserving application state. Handle EINTR, EAGAIN, EOF and other failures distinctly; one chunk is not a complete draining policy.
concepts.assumptions: For edge-triggered readiness the descriptor is nonblocking and drained until EAGAIN, EOF or failure.
concepts.counterexample: Processing only one chunk can leave unread bytes without a new edge to wake the loop.

concepts.title: Level and edge are different progress contracts
concepts.scenario: A descriptor stays readable while input remains.
concepts.explanation: Level-triggered notification can recur for a persistent condition. Neither model reserves bytes for one thread or authorizes arbitrary data received from a peer.
concepts.assumptions: Level-triggered readiness can recur while work remains; readiness is not a promise the next operation cannot race.
concepts.counterexample: Readiness does not reserve bytes for one consumer, so another thread can change the condition before read.

orientation.heading: Readiness is an opportunity to try I/O
orientation.prerequisite: Recall nonblocking I/O, partial messages and event-loop connection state from the networking chapters.

reflection_answer: Yes. Readiness can race and does not guarantee a complete message. Attempt nonblocking I/O and interpret bytes, EAGAIN, EOF and other errors according to their contracts.
security_connection: A bounded event loop must clean up failed connections and avoid an endless busy retry when no progress is available. Readiness is a progress notification, not a permission grant or a guarantee that a peer’s request is safe.

title: Pseudoterminals
reading: A program displaying a terminal window wants to exchange bytes with a shell while letting that shell use ordinary terminal behavior such as line editing and job control.
summary: A program displaying a terminal window wants to exchange bytes with a shell while letting that shell use ordinary terminal behavior such as line editing and job control..
prompt: How does a terminal emulator make a shell behave as if it has a terminal?
explanation: That program is a terminal emulator. A pseudoterminal, or PTY, has a master endpoint and a slave endpoint. The emulator communicates at the master. A shell or other program uses the slave, which supplies terminal behavior rather than behaving as an ordinary pipe alone.

Bytes written at one side are handled under the PTY/terminal rules before they are observed at the other. Line processing, echo and signal-generating characters depend on the terminal settings. Session and controlling-terminal setup establish the shell’s job-control relationship separately from opening the pair.

The emulator must also propagate window-size changes under the relevant interface and manage owned descriptors and child completion. This final chapter combines communication with terminal and lifecycle state. Creating a terminal-like channel does not change the shell’s credentials or restrict its file/network access.

concepts.title: Master and slave have different roles
concepts.scenario: An emulator relays bytes between a user and a shell.
concepts.explanation: The master transports the controller’s side of the exchange; the slave has terminal line-discipline behavior. Opening a pair alone does not complete session and controlling-terminal setup.
concepts.assumptions: A PTY slave’s terminal behavior and controlling-terminal setup are distinct from its master’s byte transport.
concepts.counterexample: A pseudoterminal does not itself change credentials or restrict file/network authority.

concepts.title: Window size and cleanup
concepts.scenario: The terminal emulator window changes size.
concepts.explanation: Window-size updates and resulting foreground-job notification follow ioctl/terminal contracts. Close owned endpoints, collect owned children and restore surrounding terminal state through explicit normal and error cleanup.
concepts.assumptions: Window-size propagation and owned descriptor/child cleanup are implemented separately; PTYs do not confer filesystem isolation.
concepts.counterexample: A robust emulator needs lifecycle and error handling beyond a successful open of the pair.

orientation.heading: Give a shell a terminal connection
orientation.prerequisite: Recall terminal settings from Chapter 62 and sessions/foreground process groups from Chapter 34.

reflection_answer: The shell uses the PTY slave as a terminal endpoint, while the emulator drives the master side. Correct terminal settings and session/controlling-terminal setup supply behavior beyond a byte pipe.
security_connection: A PTY lets a controller interact with terminal behavior and a foreground job. It is not a filesystem or network restriction: the shell’s credentials, inherited references and other policies still govern its access. Terminal emulation and containment remain separate responsibilities.
